## The characters' ranking

**The richest characters** (decided 19 October 2026). At the end of a game, beside the kings' standings, the characters are ranked by wealth: purse and hoard, what they hold. Back pay and debt tablets count for nothing at the end, as for the kings ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice"), so a loan or a fee pays only once it is paid. It shows the second game played under the kings', in which every character has a victory of his own ("Stakes, not dispositions"). During play a character knows its own wealth, not the ranking. The dead are ranked below every living character, and among themselves by what they held when they died. Dying never beats surviving, however much was held, which is the price of risk ("No age in this game"). The built ranking counts back pay owed and leaves the dead out until item 11a changes both.

**One scoreboard for every person** (decided 31 October 2026, build order item 17b; Haakon: "What if everyone are characters, even kings... Then everyone operate by the same win condition", and "if you die, it's game over"; then "Yes, please. Experlty to all!"). From item 17b the powers' scoreboard and the characters' ranking above become one, and a king is a person like any other. Every person is ranked by the same measure: what he holds, blended with how he did against par for his own start ("One scoreboard for every power"), half and half as a first guess, tuned in item 18 so that every state, Great Kings, city-states and vassals alike, has about the same chance of first place and a character wins now and then. A king's holding is his realm, the wealth of the land he holds, governed provinces included ("The wealth of a realm"); a vassal's is his own; a character's is his purse, hoard and goods. Every person, played by script, model or human, plays to rank as high as he can. Death ends a person's game and ranks him below every living one, as above, so life is worth guarding: a king dies only by a cause the record shows, where he is (in battle, at sea in a storm, in a city that falls, by a knife), never by dice or by age within the age ("No age in this game"), and a captured king's fate is his captor's to decide (ransom, hostage, release as a vassal, or death), while his skills may let him escape. When a king dies, his player is out, and the realm passes to an heir who appears only then, out of the royal house that stands in the background: the sources' named heir where the dossiers know one, otherwise a son or brother drawn as facts, as newcomers are; his score is measured from his accession, against what he inherited. No heir exists before, so nobody gains on the scoreboard by a king's death; a throne can still be taken by force, by the ledger and by broken oaths ("Loyalty is a ledger").

**Scores.** Characters rank by gold, by weight, since gold is what wealth is kept in. The lean, still open, is that goods count for nothing until sold, so a warehouse of copper is a bet against the random ending, and the omens push merchants to sell; one rule for every ranking would instead count a character's goods at reference prices, as a realm's are, and that choice stays open with the lean. Kings are settled ("The wealth of a realm"), which answers the worry that gold, now an input to almost everything, would be counted twice or reward hoarding; and since gold sent abroad, and fees paid to characters, leave the realm, darkening omens push kings neither to hoard nor to spend, but to stop paying for what will not return before the end. Item 18 tunes how much the land weighs against gold and goods, and compares win rates per power, whether Egypt spends its gold, and what the last seasons look like, so that every king has about an equal shot. When trade is built, its own balance pass checks that goods actually flow along the routes.
